events.note: Authored by an AI agent run from RFC 4648 (rfc-editor-org-0da70d4b9a) read on 2026-10-03, before any scanner was consulted; not reviewed. The evidence basis is unresolved: no source settles whether or where an encoded credential must be covered; a maintainer decision is needed.

Decided 2026-10-04 by the sole maintainer (Milo Kang, milocosmopolitan, repository owner), ADR 0019 item 2 (#94). This scenario decides the single-layer inputs (32 fixtures) and, through its twins, the 12 benign encoded inputs of the same plan, which stay must-not-flag. Question: When a credential's bytes appear in an input only after Base64 or hex encoding (one layer, or stacked up to the corpus limit of three layers and 1 KB), must the encoded text be protected, and which source range stands for it? Options: A: the decoded base is a credential, so the whole encoded text is the range and the outcome is must-flag. B: a qualified may-flag (not an outcome; ADR 0016 adds none). C: keep unresolved. Decision: A. When the decoded base value is a credential, the whole encoded text (all layers) is the secret range and the outcome is must-flag, in every layer and carrier; each span keeps `decoded` (codec steps, base sha256, byte length). Where the decoded base is not a credential (public text, a digest, a redacted mask) the encoded text stays must-not-flag, the same policy applied to the twins. Decode depth, expansion and size limits, decoder support and the action taken stay with the product. Reason: RFC 4648 defines the representations and says nothing about confidentiality. Encoding is not protection, and a rule that covers only plaintext would let an encoded copy of a credential pass. Project policy, not a provider rule or a fact. Finalized by the sole maintainer alone under the solo-maintainer period (ADR 0020): not reviewed, not independent validation, queued for retro-review (#154). Recorded by an AI agent on the owner's instruction.
events.dissent: The policy makes the corpus score decoding ability, not credential detection: a scanner that does not decode every run of Base64 or hex it sees is counted as missing 47 must-flag inputs, while the repository's own benign-encoded policy says high-entropy encoded text is not by itself a credential. RFC 4648 is silent, so nothing but the maintainer's choice separates an encoded credential from an encoded blob, and the same encoded bytes are must-flag or must-not-flag only by which authored base produced them. A product may reasonably decide not to decode at all.
events.reversingEvidence: A reliable false-positive report on decoded text (a decoded run that is not a credential but was protected under this policy), or a standard or provider statement that an encoding gives confidentiality or that an encoded form is not the credential. A product choice not to decode is not reversing evidence.

notes: Project-authored by the Redact Secret project, which maintains this repository; not independent evidence. Draft; not yet reviewed.
